title: Fed Officials Logan and Musalem Say More Rate Hikes Are Needed Soon
excerpt: Logan calls for at least two more quarter-point hikes and Musalem for firming 'soon,' days after the FOMC held rates at 3.75 percent to 4.00 percent.
body:
• Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said the Fed needs at least two more quarter-point hikes, putting the policy rate at least 50 basis points below a modestly restrictive level.
  • St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said additional firming will be necessary "and soon," with inflation still too high versus the 2 percent target.
  • The FOMC held rates at 3.75 percent to 4.00 percent this week by 10-2, after a quarter-point hike in September; two members dissented for a hike.
  • For borrowers and investors, the next decision is December 8-9 — mortgage, auto and credit-card rates are unlikely to ease if officials follow through.

Two Federal Reserve officials said on Friday that the central bank will need to raise interest rates again in coming months, on the first day officials could speak publicly after this week's decision to hold policy steady.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking at Davidson College, said the Fed needs to implement "at least" two more quarter-point hikes, according to MarketWatch via Morningstar. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, in a speech to economists in New York, also backed further increases, Reuters reported.

What Logan and Musalem said

"I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon."

— Alberto Musalem, St. Louis Fed President

"I currently estimate that the fed-funds target range is at least 50 basis points — half a percentage point — below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target," Logan said. Without at least two more hikes, she added, inflation will continue to trend above the Fed's 2 percent target unless an unexpected shock, such as a downturn, intervenes. She said the Fed could pause after those moves and reassess.

Musalem said it was his base case that inflation will only come down if there are more rate hikes. "Incremental adjustments made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger and abrupt actions taken later," he said, adding that moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or growth. He said monetary policy and financial conditions remain accommodative.

Context: a hold, after a September hike

The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 this week to leave the target range unchanged at 3.75 percent to 4.00 percent. Two policymakers dissented in favor of a rate hike. In September, the Fed had raised rates by a quarter point to that range — its first hike in three years — and at that meeting 16 of 18 officials penciled in another hike this year, MarketWatch reported.

Chairman Kevin Warsh said at his press conference that officials wanted to wait for more data before acting. Warsh, who has been reluctant to provide guidance on the outlook, did not say what he thought the Fed would do at the December 8-9 meeting, according to Reuters. Logan said she supported this week's pause because raising rates gradually "can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary." She added: "Skipping a meeting does not change the monetary-policy destination."

Other voices, and the balance of risks

Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin did not specifically say whether he would back more hikes. He noted there could be a case for higher rates if artificial-intelligence spending continued at a strong pace, telling Sirius XM that a continued surge in demand would be "the kind of thing you might want to lean against." He also supported moving slowly, saying gradual tightening makes sense when the Fed is "not much behind the curve."

Musalem does not currently have a vote on the policy-setting committee but will be a voter in 2027, Reuters noted. Logan voted on Wednesday to keep rates unchanged.

What happens next

The next FOMC meeting is December 8-9. Financial markets expect another increase in short-term borrowing costs at that meeting, according to Reuters. If Logan's path prevails, two further quarter-point moves would lift the target range to 4.25 percent to 4.50 percent before any pause to reassess — a path readers with floating-rate debt or pending mortgage decisions should price in now, rather than assuming cuts.
